excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: I graduated with a bunch of student debt and my company didn't take off. So, I was living in my parents' basement with literally $2.50 in my bank account. I had put all my eggs in one basket, thinking that this company was going to be a multi-billion dollar success, because you have to be delusional as a founder. I was left with nothing. Fortunately, I was at my parents' house, so I started building Shopify stores and taking on random freelance gigs as a self-taught developer
excerpts.context: Tyler describing his situation after college graduation when his startup failed

excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: I became very fascinated with Shopify. I thought it was such a powerful platform. I ended up doing a lot of freelance work building Shopify sites
excerpts.context: Tyler explaining his early freelance work with Shopify

excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: My good buddy Austin Rief who is also from Baltimore called me
excerpts.context: Tyler describing how Austin first contacted him

excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: I was on an hour-long car ride home from DC and Austin was venting [on the call] about the business and the opportunity. This was when Morning Brew probably had 30,000-40,000 subscribers. He was debating raising money and going full time or taking a big investment banking job in New York. One thing he said was, 'Did you know Barstool is making 40% of their revenue through merch?' or whatever the number was. He was interested in merch, and I said, 'Dude, I got you.' Shopify was my thing. I said, 'Let me help you build,' because they had some brand affinity with the mug and the logo, and people wanted t-shirts, hats, or coffee mugs. So the first idea was, 'I'll help you build a Shopify store'
excerpts.context: Tyler describing the initial conversation with Austin that led to working for Morning Brew

excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: We started talking, and he said theSkimm is growing so quickly. They were trailblazers in the newsletter space, with millions of subscribers. They had the Skimm'bassadors program, a referral program that worked really well. All these girls in New York who read it loved their ambassador program and were always sharing it. He said, 'We should imitate that'
excerpts.context: Austin (via Tyler) discussing theSkimm's success and referral program model

excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: I straight-faced told him, 'Yeah, absolutely, no problem.' Even though I had no idea how to do it. I had $2.50 in my bank account and he offered me $3,000 to do it
excerpts.context: Tyler accepting his first contract work from Austin despite not knowing how to build what was requested

excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: For 3 weeks, I was building this referral program, making it up as I went. I had no idea what I was doing and almost quit 5 separate times. At 2 a.m., I'd be up thinking, 'I lied about being able to do this, and I have no idea how to get past this point.' I almost texted him to give up but didn't. I finished it and he paid me $3,000
excerpts.context: Tyler describing the struggle of building his first referral program for Morning Brew

excerpts.speaker: tyler_denk
excerpts.quote_text: Then [Austin] said, 'We have so many other projects to build. If you want to keep working with us throughout the summer while you apply for full-time jobs, let's do it.' So I started contracting for them, working 40-60 hours a week, building the website, improving the referral program, and creating different components for the newsletter
excerpts.context: Austin extending Tyler's contract work throughout the summer
